summary: The note recounts the folklore of the Witch of the Willow Woods, also called Sybilla, beginning with Elsie Carmichael's encounter at an old cottage while searching for her lost cat. It covers tales of both blessings and curses, the woods' seasonal character, the legend's cultural impact (documentary, festival, ballads), the surviving cottage, and varied villager beliefs. No concrete evidence of the witch exists, yet the legend endures through oral tradition.
one_line: Folklore of Sybilla, the Witch of the Willow Woods: her first sighting, good and ill deeds, cultural legacy, cottage, and villagers' differing beliefs.
key_facts: The legend of the Witch of the Willow Woods is said to have first been recounted on September 13th, 2024.
Elsie Carmichael entered the Willow Woods looking for her lost cat and found an old, crooked cottage where she met a cloaked figure, a benevolent witch.
Elsie's account was published on October 2nd, 2024, in the Willow Weekly.
Villagers later named the witch "Sybilla of the Willow Woods."
Thomas Fletcher (December 5th, 2025) told of crop blessings after a ritualistic dance in the woods; Ada Bell (January 14th, 2026) said the witch's potions and herbs cured her ailing grandmother.
On March 9th, 2027, botanist Dr. Richard Grove disappeared after trespassing in the woods to collect rare flora, which was attributed to the witch's ire.
The documentary "Whispers of the Witch" aired on June 6th, 2028, to rave reviews.
A festival in the witch's honor began on September 20th, 2029, celebrating the autumn equinox.
The cottage is overgrown with moss and vines, lacks electricity and running water, and local historian James Howitt dated its architecture to the early 1700s.
Despite numerous investigations, no concrete evidence corroborates the witch's existence.
Mrs. Abigail Turner sees the witch as a boogeyman to keep children from the woods, while Will O'Donnell sees her as nature's untouched beauty and wrath.
Mayor Richard Snyder admitted in a May 10th, 2030 interview to occasionally placing offerings at the woods' entrance hoping for a bountiful year.
In winter, the bare willow branches are said to be the witch's sentinels.
